Enhanced methane production and energy potential from rice straw
by employing microaerobic pretreatment via anaerobic digestion

This study employs a microaerobic pretreatment that includes different microbial reagents combined
with oxygen to enhance the energy conversion potential of rice straw (RS) via anaerobic digestion (AD) in
a more cost-effective and time-efﬁcient manner. Five broad varieties of microbial reagents including
liquid consortium (LC), cow manure (CM), sheep dung (SD), biogas slurry (BS), and straw-decomposing
consortia (SC), have been used as sources of useful microbes at varying oxygen concentrations of 0, 6, 12
and 24 mLO2/gVS to explore the effect of microaerobic pretreatment on RS degradation. The results
showed that RS pretreated with SC had the highest cumulative methane yield (CMY) of 311.7 mL/gVS at
12 mLO2/gVS, followed by BS, CM, LC, and SD, with the CMYs of 270.5, 263.2, 257.1, and 256.7 mL/gVS at 6
mLO2/gVS, respectively. The RS pretreated with SC, BS, CM, LC, and SD led to improvements in the
methane yield by 88.7%, 63.7%, 59.3%, 55.6%, and 55.4%, respectively, compared to the untreated RS. The
microbial community analysis revealed that the relative abundance (RA) of Firmicutes, which are known
to play a key role in accelerating the rate of hydrolysis, increased after microbial pretreatment combined
with oxygen supply. The RA of Clostridium III, which facilitates cell wall degradation via hydrolytic
pathways along with other sugar-fermenting bacteria, such as Saccharofermentans, Lutaonella, and Sed-
imentibacter, increased after AD in the digestate of pretreated RS compared to that in untreated RS.
Moreover, a shift in acetoclastic and hydrogenotrophic archaea, including Methanothrix and Meth-
anospirillum, was also observed, indicating precursor changes resulted by pretreatments and varied
microbial metabolism, which might have enhanced the methane production process of RS. The energy
potential analysis revealed that microbial pretreatment was a suitable technique for stimulating the
energy conversion efﬁciency of RS. This study can be used as a reference for future utilization of a diverse
range of lignocellulosic materials for clean energy production.

1. Introduction
Rapid economic development and increasing population have
led to a growing energy demand, with global energy consumption
reaching 12.93 billion tons in 2014 (Mustafa et al., 2016). Nonre-
newable energy in the form of fossil fuels accounted for 86.3% of the
total energy consumption worldwide, whereas renewable energy
accounted for only 9.2%. The high dependency on fossil fuels has
resulted in increased greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions and thus
contributed
to
climate
change,
eventually
causing
adverse
environmental impacts. Hence, there is a dire need to develop
environmentally friendly and cost-effective alternative energy
sources to meet the growing energy demand, one of which is
biomass energy (Li et al., 2019). Different types of feedstocks,
including agricultural waste, municipal solid waste (MSW), indus-
trial waste, etc., are used as biomass energy sources to produce
biomethane via anaerobic digestion (AD), which is a cost-effective
technology adopted for clean energy production (Jingura and
Kamusoko, 2017; Xin et al., 2020).
Rice straw (RS) is a lignocellulosic biomass that is abundantly
generated in China, with a total yield of 213 million tons in 2017
(Xia et al., 2018). RS consists of a complex matrix of cellulose,
hemicellulose, and lignin, which makes it more recalcitrant to
biodegradation (Huang et al., 2020). Therefore, several pretreat-
ment methods have been studied for removing these barriers and

enhancing the enzymatic hydrolysis of RS to improve its energy
output in the form of biomethane.
To date, physical, chemical, and biological pretreatments have
been widely applied to pretreat RS (Guan et al., 2018). Physical
methods are applied to reduce the particle size of the substrate,
whereas chemical pretreatment involves the use of chemicals to
enhance biomass digestibility; however, these pretreatments have
high energy costs and require careful handling (Harmsen et al.,
2010; Li et al., 2015). Biological pretreatment is an environmen-
tally friendly and cost-effective method that employs fungi to
degrade lignocellulosic components via the action of various useful
enzymes (Saritha et al., 2012). The use of fungi reduces pretreat-
ment cost because these organisms are capable of degrading lignin
with the help of ligninolytic enzymes; however, the degradation
rate is slow. Hence, a longer pretreatment time and higher oxygen
consumption are required during fungal pretreatment (Kamusoko
et al., 2019). Therefore, it is important to ﬁnd an effective method
with a shorter pretreatment time for faster hydrolysis of lignocel-
lulosic components. As reported in a previous study, microaerobic
pretreatment is a time-efﬁcient method that requires a shorter
pretreatment time than other methods. During this pretreatment
process, microorganisms are partially exposed to oxygen under
moderate operating parameters. The process accelerates the hy-
drolysis stage by stimulating microbial activity and cell growth
(Botheju and Bakke, 2011; Fu et al., 2015; Montalvo et al., 2016;
Wagner et al., 2018; Xu et al., 2018). Although oxygen may help
regulate the microbial community structure, it is still challenging to
balance the positive and negative effects of microaeration during
AD. Moreover, detailed analysis of the mechanisms involved in the
microaerobic pretreatment is also required to further understand
the process.
To carry out the microaerobic pretreatment, this study chose
different types of microbial reagents that contain complex mixtures
of useful microorganisms belonging to different growth environ-
ments and are known to play a key role in hydrolyzing cellulose.
These microorganism-rich reagents, including liquid consortium
(LC), cow manure (CM), sheep dung (SD), biogas slurry (BS), and
straw-decomposing consortia (SC), were used as a potential source
of different microbes to investigate the microbial pretreatment
effects on the AD performance of RS. This study proposed an
economical microaerobic pretreatment method for the efﬁcient
degradation of lignocellulosic substrates with reduced pretreat-
ment time while enhanced methane production. It also established
the connection between the oxygen supply and microbial functions
and how this interaction impacts the rate of hydrolysis.
The main objectives of this study are: (1) developing a sus-
tainable pretreatment method by using different microbial re-
agents and oxygen levels to enhance the methane production
performance of RS, (2) investigating the changes in the microbial
communities before pretreatment, after pretreatment, and after AD
to study the response of functional microorganisms to varying
oxygen concentrations, and (3) carrying out energy potential ana-
lyses that consider different microbial reagents and their respective
biomethane yields.
2. Materials and methods
2.1. Feedstock and inoculum
RS was collected from a farm located in Henan Province of
China, and it was chopped to a size of less than 1 cm and ground by
a high-speed grinder (XINGSHILIHE, Beijing, China). Sheep dung
(SD) and cow manure (CM) were collected from farms in Shunyi
District, Beijing, China, and deionized water was added to each
manure to make a homogenous mixture. Liquid consortium (LC)
and straw-decomposing consortia (SC) are commercially available
and were purchased for this experiment. Biogas slurry (BS) used as
the startup inoculum for AD was obtained from the Beijing Dong-
huashan Biogas Plant.
2.2. Analytical methods
Total solids (TS) and volatile solids (VS) of the feedstock and
inoculum were analyzed as per standard methods (APHA, 2005).
The substrates were weighed and placed in an oven at 105 C for
24 h to remove moisture and weighed again. The TS content was
calculated from the weight difference, as shown in Eq. (1). The dried
samples were placed in a mufﬂe furnace at 550 C for 2 h, and then
they were removed, placed in a desiccator, cooled to room tem-
perature, and weighed. The VS content was calculated as shown in
Eq. (2).

2.3. Effects of microbial reagents and oxygen on the pretreatment of
rice straw
Pretreatment was performed in triplicate using RS with an
organic loading of 20 g VS/L. 5 mL LC and 4 g VS/L CM, SD, BS, and SC
were separately used as microbial reagents to pretreat the RS.
Deionized water was added to achieve a working volume of 100 mL,
and the retention time was 24 h. N2 was ﬂushed in each bottle for
3 min to ensure the removal of air, and rubber stoppers were used
to seal the bottles. Then, controlled oxygen concentrations of 0, 6,
12, and 24 mLO2/gVS were injected into the AD digesters. The
bottles were then placed in an incubator at 37 C. A gas chro-
matograph (7890B, Agilent, USA) was used to measure oxygen and
CO2 concentration every 6 h until all oxygen was completely used.
2.4. Anaerobic digestion
AD was performed in triplicate. When all the oxygen was
consumed, the concentrated inoculum was inoculated into the
pretreated RS at a feedstock to inoculum ratio of 1. A working
volume of 0.25 L was achieved using deionized water. The digesters
were purged with high-purity N2 to ensure anaerobic condition,
after which they were sealed and placed in a 37 C incubator for 50
days. Three blank digesters (control group) were used to subtract
background CH4 from the test group. All digesters were shaken at a
speed of 130 rpm every day for 1 min before testing the biogas
pressure. A schematic illustration of the experimental design is
shown in Fig. 1.

2.8. Energy potential analysis
The energy potential analysis was evaluated in the form of en-
ergy density and total energy yield (Passos et al., 2017; Shen et al.,
2019).
2.9. Statistical analysis
All the data and graphs were processed using Origin Pro 9.0
(Origin Lab, USA). An analysis of variance (ANOVA) was used to
statistically analyze the data.

3.2. Variations in O2 and CO2 concentration during microbial
pretreatment
Oxygen was supplied at four different concentrations of 0, 6, 12,
and 24 mLO2/gVS to explore its effect on the microbial community
structure in the digester. Microbes play an important role in hy-
drolyzing
polysaccharides
into
monosaccharides,
which
are
partially converted into CO2 with the supply of oxygen (Sadhu and
Maiti, 2013; Shallom and Shoham, 2003). All oxygen was consumed
in 24 h by different microbial reagents, namely, LC, CM, SD, BS, and
SC, as shown in Fig. 2. At an oxygen concentration of 6 mLO2/gVS,
the fastest consumption of oxygen was observed by SC in 6 h, fol-
lowed by CM and BS in 12 h, while LC and SD consumed all the
oxygen in 18 h. At the oxygen concentration of 12 mLO2/gVS, the
fastest consumption of oxygen was again observed by SC in 6 h,
followed by CM and BS, which took 18 h for oxygen consumption,
while LC and SD consumed all the oxygen in 24 h. At the oxygen
concentration of 24 mLO2/gVS, SC consumed all the oxygen in 12 h,
followed by LC, CM, SD, and BS, which took 24 h to consume all the
oxygen. Accordingly, in LC, CM, SD and BS, a rise in CO2 content was
seen, which shows that microbes present in these microbial re-
agents had moderate metabolic activity, while the CO2 content in
SC showed rapid metabolism during the oxygen supply, thus con-
ﬁrming a high activity of microbial communities. Hence, the
degradation of RS pretreated by different microbial reagents in the
presence of oxygen can be evaluated by the production of CO2. A
previous report indicated that during pretreatment of lignocellu-
losic material, cellulose and hemicellulose could be depolymerized
to glucose and xylose, which were further utilized by microor-
ganisms to produce CO2 in the aerobic environment (Lu et al., 2019;
Shallom and Shoham, 2003), whereas lignin might be converted to
vanillic acid by adopting different pathways and transformed into
pyruvic and a-ketobutyric acid (Bugg et al., 2011).
3.3. VFAs and pH after pretreatment
The changes in VFAs and pH after pretreatment are shown in
Fig. 3F. The desirable VFAs produced during pretreatment are acetate
and butyrate, which contribute to methane production; however, the
generation of other VFAs, such as valeric and propionic acid, is
known to limit the process of methane production (Xu et al., 2014).
The total VFAs after pretreatment with different microbial reagents
in the absence of oxygen, such as LC, CM, SD, BS, and SC, were found
to be 1345.4, 2105.7, 2140.9, 2431.4, and 2032.2 mg/L, respectively. At
the oxygen concentration of 6 mLO2/gVS, the highest VFAs concen-
trations in the pretreated groups by LC, CM, SD, and BS were 2440.0,
2506.3, 2937.8, and 2810.0 mg/L, respectively, whereas for the SC
pretreated group, the concentration of VFAs was the highest
(2525.9 mg/L) at 12 mLO2/gVS. This ﬁnding indicated a signiﬁcant
increase in VFAs production, which was observed when microbial
pretreatment was combined with oxygen. This might be attributed
to the enrichment of Firmicutes and Bacteroidetes during pretreat-
ment, which requires further veriﬁcation by detailed study on mi-
crobial community analysis. As microbes belonging to these two
phyla
mostly contain
hydrolytic
bacteria,
which
might
have
contributed to the hydrolysis of macromolecules to produce VFAs at
a faster pace, therefore, a higher VFAs concentration was achieved.
Furthermore, the concentrations of acetate and butyrate were the
top two highest in all groups pretreated with microbial reagents
except for the SD-pretreated group, which had the highest concen-
tration of propionic acid at 430e990 mg/L. This difference might lead
to the lower methane yield of the SD-pretreated group compared to
the other pretreated groups because previous studies have reported
that a higher concentration of propionic acid adversely affects the
function of methanogenic bacteria and thereby lowers the methane
yield (Lee et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2009). At an oxygen concentration
of 24 mLO2/gVS during pretreatment, the concentration of total VFAs
decreased, which might be due to the oxidation of readily available
VFAs during oxygen pretreatment. These results are consistent with
the ﬁndings of a previous study that supplied oxygen into the AD
digester while treating food waste (Xu et al., 2014). The initial pH of

3.4. Effect of microbial pretreatment on methane production
3.4.1. Daily methane yield (DMY)
The main purpose of microbial pretreatment is to enhance the
methane yield by accelerating the AD process. The daily methane
yield (DMY) of RS after pretreatment with various microbial re-
agents is shown in Fig. 3. The maximum DMYs of RS pretreated by
LC under oxygen concentrations of 0, 6, 12, and 24 mLO2/gVS were
11.5, 22.3, 16.6, and 19.6 mL/gVS on the 3rd day, respectively
(Fig. 3A). The maximum DMYs of RS pretreated with CM under
different oxygen concentrations were 12.8, 33.0, 21.1, and 18.3 mL/
gVS on the 3rd day (Fig. 3B), respectively, whereas the maximum
DMYs of RS pretreated with SD for all oxygen concentrations were
13.2, 24, 14.1, and 11.1 mL/gVS between the 3rd and 5th days
(Fig. 3C). The maximum DMYs of RS pretreated with BS for various
oxygen concentrations were 12.3, 24.7, 16, and 13.5 mL/gVS on the
4th day (Fig. 3D), whereas the maximum DMY for the untreated
group was 15.8 mL/gVS recorded on the 6th day, after which
methane production declined and became stable from the 16th day
onwards. Nevertheless, a different trend was observed in the pre-
treatment of RS by SC, where the oxygen concentrations of 0, 6, 12,
and 24 mLO2/gVS led to signiﬁcantly higher DMY values of 24.8,
26.6, 31.5, and 24.5 mL/gVS on the 4th day compared with the un-
treated group, respectively (Fig. 3E). The pretreatment of RS by
different microbial reagents, such as LC, CM, SD and BS, showed

3.4.2. Cumulative methane yield (CMY)
The highest CMY values of RS pretreated by the microbial re-
agents LC, CM, SD, BS, and SC without oxygen were 200.8, 182.0,
193.5, 203.0, and 267.7 mL/gVS, respectively, as shown in Fig. 4.
When oxygen was combined with the microbial pretreatment, a
further increase in the CMY values was observed. For example, the
highest CMYs of RS pretreated with LC, CM, SD, and BS were 257.1,
263.2, 256.7, and 270 mL/gVS at the optimal oxygen concentration
of 6 mLO2/gVS, whereas the highest CMY value of RS pretreated
with SC was 311.7 mL/gVS at the optimal oxygen concentration of
12 mLO2/gVS. The improvement in the yield by only using LC, CM,
SD, BS, and SC was 21.5, 10.2, 17.1, 22.9, and 62.0%, respectively,
whereas the applying oxygen led to an increase in the methane
yield by 55.6, 59.3, 55.4, 63.7, and 88.7% compared to URS,
respectively. An increase in the oxygen concentration beyond the
suitable range has a negative effect on the methane yield due to the
excess consumption of substrate by facultative organisms under
high oxygen levels. Among all reagents, SC outperformed BS, CM,
LC, and SD at oxygen concentrations of 12 and 6 mLO2/gVS.
Mshandete et al. (2005) reported a 26% higher methane yield from
sisal pulp after 9 h of microaerobic pretreatment. Zhu et al. (2009)
also reported an increase in the hydrolysis rate during the methane
production process by employing a sufﬁcient amount of oxygen.
The improvement yield obtained in this study is much higher than
previously reported values.

The changes in the ﬁber composition of RS pretreated by

treatment by LC, CM, SD, BS, and SC, the proportion of cellulose
increased (34.7 ± 0.3%, 41.8 ± 0.2%, 40.9 ± 0.7%, 40.7 ± 0.5%, and
45.3 ± 0.0%, respectively) compared to the URS (33.9 ± 0.4%),
indicating that the lignin content decreased and that cellulose was
more accessible to the microbes for breakdown and conversion to
the end products of AD. After providing an oxygen supply, a further
increase in the proportion of cellulose to 49.6 ± 0.5%, 48.5 ± 0.4%,

concentration of 12 mLO2/gVS for all groups except BS, which
showed the highest proportion of cellulose at 6 mLO2/gVS. Micro-

helping to release not only cellulose but also hemicellulose, as
shown in Table 2. After AD, the proportion of cellulose decreased
signiﬁcantly. An increase in lignin content after AD can be ascribed
to the degradation of the other components (cellulose and hemi-
cellulose) from RS, thus increasing the relative content of lignin in
the digestate (Kong et al., 2018). The results showed that the surface
structure of RS was loosen after pretreatment with different mi-
crobial reagents in the presence of oxygen and became more
accessible to anaerobic bacteria, which promoted the effective hy-
drolysis of RS.

combined with oxygen, a further increase was observed. For

rose to 59.4, 60.8, 59.3, and 62.5%, respectively, whereas the BD of
SC treated group was the highest at 72.0% under an oxygen con-

pretreatments facilitated the biodegradation of RS and the combi-

3.9. Microbial community diversity after AD
3.9.1. Species diversity and richness
Table 3 shows the richness and diversity estimators, such as the
sequence, OTU number, Shannon, ACE, and Chao1 indexes for
bacteria and archaea. The ACE and Chao1 indexes indicate richness,
whereas the Shannon index indicates the diversity of microbes (Zhi

sequencing depth for all samples was sufﬁcient to cover the whole
diversity, which was conﬁrmed by the coverage values of 98e99%

4. Energy potential analysis and practical implications
According to the conclusions from the methane yield, an energy
potential analysis was carried out to compare the AD performance
of different microbial reagents used to enhance the energy output
of RS.
4.1. Energy potential analysis
The energy potential analysis of the RS after microaerobic pre-
treatment was calculated. Among all the microbial reagents used for
pretreatment, the SC pretreatment of RS showed the highest energy
density (8.67  103 kJ kg1), followed by BS (7.52  103 kJ kg1), CM
(7.32  103 kJ kg1),LC (7.15  103 kJkg1), and SD (7.14  103 kJ kg1),
whereas the energy density of URS was 4.59  103 kJ kg1. In China,
the yield of RS was estimated to be 213 million tons (Xia et al., 2018); if
this amount of RS is converted to bioenergy via AD after microbial
pretreatment, the overall energy yield is estimated to be in the range
of 1.52  1012-1.85  1012 MJ/year using different microbial reagents.
This ﬁnding indicated that there is a huge energy potential for
implementing microbial pretreatment in AD of RS.
4.2. Practical implication
The microbial pretreatment technique facilitates the biocon-
version of organic matter to biomethane by providing a practical
pretreatment method for lignocellulosic material through utilizing
readily available microbial reagents along with an oxygen supply to
enhance the methane yield. Additionally, the residual digestate
from AD can be used as an organic fertilizer, thereby promoting
nutrient recovery and crop production.
5. Conclusions
Microaerobic pretreatment represents an effective pretreatment
method for the biodegradation of RS with enhanced methane
production during AD. All ﬁve microbial reagents, namely, SC, BS,
CM, LC, and SD, represented sources of useful bacteria and led to an
increase in methane yield by 88.7%, 63.7%, 59.3%, 55.6%, and 55.4%,
respectively. The most suitable oxygen concentrations were 6 and
12 mLO2/gVS and increases in oxygen concentration beyond these
values led to a decrease in the methane yield. The results of the
microbial community analysis showed that the use of microbial
reagents improved the microbial diversity in the AD digester. When
microbial reagents with varying oxygen concentrations were used,
the microbial population was further enriched, which eventually
led to enhanced methane production performance. The microbial
community analysis revealed that the RA of Firmicutes increased
after microaerobic pretreatment, which is known to play a key role
in accelerating the rate of hydrolysis. The RA of Clostridium III,
which facilitates cell wall degradation by following hydrolytic
pathways, along with that of other sugar-fermenting bacteria, such
as Saccharofermentans, Lutaonella, and Sedimentibacter, increased
after AD in the digestate of pretreated RS compared to the URS. The

pretreated RS compared to the URS. This result indicated that
pretreatments led to changes in microbial metabolism, which
eventually caused a shift in methanogen pathways, such as aceto-
clastic, hydrogenotrophic, and methylotrophic pathways, and
therefore impacted the methane production process. SC was found
to be the most efﬁcient microbial reagent for the degradation of RS
compared to BS, CM, LC, and SD. The energy potential analysis
showed that the energy yield increased after pretreatment with all
groups (1.52 1012-1.85  1012 MJ/year) compared with the energy
yield of the URS (0.98  1012 MJ/year). This ﬁnding implies that
microbial pretreatment is a suitable technique for enhancing the
energy conversion efﬁciency of RS and a promising pretreatment
strategy for the treatment of other lignocellulosic materials for
their application in AD at the industrial scale.
